topics.title: Traditional fugue elements
topics.summary: Step 1 of any analysis: find and label the subject and answer entries (with voice and key), the countersubject(s), codettas, episodes, middle entries, any stretto, and the coda; note techniques such as augmentation, diminution, inversion and retrograde.
guidelines: Beyond the exposition you do not need to decide whether an entry is a "subject" or an "answer" — it is often impossible unless the answer is tonal (Roberts).
In Bach the voice often "runs into" the subject without a break, sometimes arriving only on its second note — a reason not to hammer every entry in performance (Badura-Skoda).

terms.def: the subject transposed to the dominant (real = exact; tonal = adjusted so the tonic–dominant frame stays in the key)
a counter-melody that regularly accompanies the subject/answer
a short link inside the exposition (Roberts follows Lester and calls the one in WTC I c minor "Episode 1")
the first round of entries, one in each voice; its end is part of Step 1
a passage without a complete entry, usually built from subject or CS motives, often sequential and modulating
entries after the exposition, often in related keys
a second exposition in which the voices that had the subject now have the answer and vice versa (Gedalge's plan)
a held bass (dominant before the end, tonic at the end in the academic plan)
closing section after the last structural cadence

sources: Roberts (2004), Ch. 3 Step 1 and Fig. 5 (WTC I C minor)
Badura-Skoda (1993), Ch. 10 "General Remarks on the Performance of Fugues"
Gedalge, Traité de la fugue (plan table)
Mann, The Study of Fugue (1958/1987), Marpurg pp. 154–155

checks: Element list = Roberts Step 1a; counterexposition and pedal points from Gedalge's plan

Cross-check (Mann): Marpurg (1753) names five characteristic elements — theme, answer, exposition (repercussio), counterparts, episodes; Walther's repercussio also meant the counter-exposition. Consistent with the list.

topics.title: How long are Bach's fugues? (statistics)
topics.summary: Roberts measures length in beats (bars × beats per bar) so that different metres compare fairly.
guidelines: Following Paul Walker: harpsichord fugues tend to be brief and tight (teaching pieces), organ fugues grander (public performance, pedal range and colour).
sources: Roberts (2004), Ch. 1 Tables 1–2; Ch. 3

checks: Averages and subject lengths quoted from Roberts; the full per-fugue tables are in the dissertation

topics.title: Six-step method for fugue analysis
topics.summary: Roberts' core idea: each Bach fugue begins with a "musical core" containing notable properties — things that arouse analytic curiosity. The rest of the fugue either reconciles them (a rhetorical approach) or leaves them unchallenged (a literal approach). The process is recursive: a property's importance only shows once you see the whole fugue.
steps: 1. Identify the traditional elements: entries (voice, key), countersubject, codettas, episodes, coda; techniques (augmentation, diminution, inversion, retrograde, stretto); harmony.

2. Find notable properties in the exposition: linear ascents/descents; "blocked" ascents/descents; rhythmic and melodic patterns (e.g. cells); "suspended" scale degrees; contrasting material (active vs static); structural units (a subject that is a period).

3. Look for patterns in the structure from Step 1, using integrants (the recurring element, usually entries) and digressions (what comes between, usually episodes): successively longer/shorter sections; mirrored (palindromic) lengths; simple length ratios (1:2, 2:3, 3:4, 4:5 — the tuning ratios).

4. Re-segment the fugue by other significant phenomena if the entry/episode map is unhelpful: incoherent or obscured entry structure; rare changes in the prevailing rhythm; rare changes of texture or density; several entries fused into one "Exposition Block".
5. If Step 4 produced a new structure, repeat Step 3 on it.

6. Decide how the fugue responds: a property is reconciled when it reappears with the feature that made it notable resolved (a blocked descent finally reaches 1̂). All reconciled → rhetorical; none → literal.
guidelines: Do not treat the expected Urlinie descent as notable by itself; it becomes notable only if the fugue makes something of it.
In the rhetorical fugues studied, the properties resolve together, near the end, and the fugue stops soon after (any coda is brief).
Accept as notable only features supported both in the opening and in the fugue as a whole.

terms.def: a salient feature not required of every fugue (e.g. a head-and-tail subject), or an anomaly
a descent that does not reach 1̂, or an ascent that stops short of 5̂ (from below) or 1̂ (from 5̂)
a non-tonic degree left unconnected linearly
the recurring core element vs what lies between; = entry / episode in a traditional segmentation
several entries that act as one unit (BWV 547)
notable properties resolved by musical "argument" / simply presented and left standing

sources: Roberts (2004), Ch. 1 and Ch. 3 (outline of the methodology)

checks: Steps and sub-points follow Roberts' own outline at the end of Ch. 3
flags: Roberts builds on Daniel Harrison ("Rhetoric and Fugue", 1990) and Joel Lester (2001); he deliberately avoids naming classical rhetorical figures.

topics.title: Other analytical approaches (and their limits)
topics.summary: Roberts surveys approaches before proposing his own.
guidelines: "No single defining characteristic beyond imitation in the broadest sense" (Walker, quoted by Roberts) — fugue is a procedure more than a form.

tables.title: Approaches to fugue analysis (Roberts, Ch. 2 and Conclusion)
rows: describes the surface; treats fugue as a form, not as a compositional process
rhythm-first readings can conflict with harmony and voice leading
paradigms do not always clarify the harmony and voice leading of a fugue
rhetoric as musical argument: a status (issue) is set up and resolved
adopted as the basis of the rhetorical reading
an opening core of material worked through parallel sections with heightened recurrences
adopted, but "core" widened beyond themes to structure, rhythm and spacing
extended to horizontal space (blocks of bars)

sources: Roberts (2004), Ch. 1–2, Conclusion

topics.title: How the old masters analysed fugues
topics.summary: Long before modern methods, fugues were analysed in print. The historical models show what earlier musicians listened for, and Mann's history shows which habits later distorted analysis.
guidelines: Marpurg's lesson from his analysis: entries should not be delayed when the texture allows them; free passages are inserted only to reach a place suited for an entry.
Martini judges a fugue by clarity, simplicity and regularity — and by whether every voice re-enters with the theme after a rest.
Mann: describe style before form; a fugue is a sum of procedures (state, answer, establish the key, develop, re-establish), not a mould.

tables.title: Historical analyses of fugues
rows: bar-by-bar account divided into seven expositions; for each: order of entries, subject/answer exchange, closeness of entries, double counterpoint, how cadences are avoided
segment a fugue into expositions and say what changes from one to the next
four "parts" defined by key areas (I–V; III–VI; vi–ii; dominant then tonic pedal) and by which themes combine
read the large form through key areas and combinations, not a fixed pattern
numbered entry markers in the score with commentary (real vs tonal answers, "inversion of answers", stretto, pedal, harmonies used)
annotate entries with numbers and comment only on what is notable
Rameau-style fundamental-bass analyses of WTC fugues (C minor, B minor) — C. P. E. Bach disclaimed Rameau's principles
harmonic reduction is one layer, not the whole story
fugue as tripartite form / 8-bar period; "exam fugue" checklists
avoid: Mann shows these judge Bach by rules his fugues never followed

sources: Mann, The Study of Fugue (1958/1987), pp. 182–184 (Marpurg's analysis), 204–212 (Kyrie), 270–312 (Martini), 62–72 (textbooks)
C. P. E. Bach, Essay (trans. Mitchell 1949), translator's introduction (Mitchell) on Kirnberger's analyses

checks: Summarised from Mann's translations; Kirnberger detail from Mitchell's introduction to the Essay

topics.title: WTC I, Fugue in C minor, BWV 847 — Roberts' demonstration
topics.summary: A three-voice, 31-bar fugue used to demonstrate the method.

properties: Prominent descent 6̂–5̂–4̂–3̂ in the subject that never reaches 1̂ (blocked)
Episode 1 (bars 5–6): an ascent 5̂→1̂ through every half step of the combined minor-scale forms
Rhythmic cells in the subject: 4+4+3+3+2 eighth notes (motive repeated, interrupted, then mirrored)
cases.structure: Entries at bars 1, 3, 7, 11, 15, 20, 26 with episodes between (Ep. 4 = inversion of Ep. 1); coda with a final subject statement
cases.resolution: Bars 27–29: the descent reaches 1̂ (soprano and bass), the 5̂→1̂ ascent goes straight up the melodic minor, and the cells shrink to 4+4+3+3+3+3+2+1 — all at once, then the fugue ends.

sources: Roberts (2004), Ch. 3 (Figs. 5–12, Table 3)

checks: Bar numbers and cells quoted from Roberts

topics.title: Four organ fugues (Roberts)
topics.summary: Each fugue shows a different kind of notable property.

properties: Subject = an asymmetrical period (2-bar phrase to HC + 2½-bar phrase to AC)
Descending arpeggio D–B♭–G and the opening fifth
cases.structure: Digressions grow additively: 2, 3, 3½, 5, 8½ bars (each later one the sum of two earlier); period V is the only expanded integrant
cases.resolution: The expansion of the subject's period is mirrored in the growing digressions, which make the last (unchanged) entry sound climactic.

cases.structure: Spacing of the eight entries: 2, 3½, 3½, 5, 5, 3½, 3½, 2 bars — a palindrome
cases.resolution: Nothing is reconciled: a "stop-and-start" fugue (Roberts reads it as frustration, or as a secure enclosure).

cases.work: C major BWV 545 — unexpected change of prevailing rhythm
properties: Slow, vocal-like subject (static) vs later running eighths
Quarter-note motion returns only at bars 18, 54, 81, 108–9
cases.structure: Those four rhythmic breaks coincide with cadences and divide the fugue in proportions close to tuning ratios (Roberts, Table 9); several entries are obscured
cases.resolution: First case where the alternative structure (Step 4) reveals the notable property.

properties: Entries fused into Exposition Blocks of three; the 4th exposition entry belongs to the transition
cases.structure: EBs shrink from three entries to two (dividing the fugue 2:1) and finally one; entries augmented, then augmented and inverted, overlapping by half their length
cases.resolution: The reduction of the blocks, ending in a single entry reinforced by a tonal answer, resolves the "combined forces".

sources: Roberts (2004), Ch. 4–7

checks: Section lengths and verdicts quoted from Roberts; BWV 545 is not explicitly labelled rhetorical or literal in the text

topics.title: WTC I, Fugue in D♯ minor, BWV 853 — an analysis for performance (Badura-Skoda)
topics.summary: A structural and affective reading aimed at the performer.
guidelines: Free "1½-times" augmentation (only some notes lengthened, bars 24–27) prepares the real augmentation — a device Bach reuses in The Art of Fugue.
Bach's inversion is not mathematically exact: harmony comes first (bar 30).

properties: Subject: 5̂ → minor 6̂ → 5̂, the "pathopoietic" figure; kinship with Luther's "Aus tiefer Not"
Second half rises only a 4th from the tonic, like a small coda; bar lines cut across a 3 + 2 grouping of minims
The minor 6th is the melodic climax even though it falls on a weak, short note
Countersubjects (unusually free) are stepwise and cantabile: a contrast to the subject's gravity
cases.structure: Surplus 4th entry in the exposition (bars 12–14); expected F♯ major evaded (bars 16–17), cadence in A♯ minor instead (bar 19), first stretto in A♯ minor; F♯ major arrives only at bar 30 with the first inversion; inversion in the bass at bar 44 = middle of the fugue (first climax); triple stretto of the subject (minor, bars 52–53) answered by triple stretto of the inversion (major); from bar 61 (HC) subject in augmentation thrice, combined with subject, inversion and a "one-and-a-half" augmentation (bar 77); Picardy third
cases.resolution: The fugue moves from the prelude's grief toward light: subject (minor) vs inversion (major) is almost programmatic; the ending should be firm, not a diminuendo.

sources: Badura-Skoda (1993), Ch. 10, pp. 220–227

flags: Badura-Skoda (with Tovey, Keller and others) thinks the fugue was first in D minor and transposed; editions printing it in E♭ minor are "perfectly reasonable".

topics.title: Key plan as the structure's corner-stones
topics.summary: Modulations to related keys are the most audible landmarks of a Bach fugue.
rules: Major: usually first to the dominant, then to more distant related keys (in C: G, then a, d, sometimes F); the mediant (e) is the most distant diatonic area and carries the most tension; keys outside the scale (B♭, D in C major) are rare.
Minor: first to the dominant and the relative major.
The last structural events are the return to the tonic and, often, dominant or tonic pedal points.
guidelines: Tension grows with distance from the tonic, "as if a rubber band were attached to the tonic" (Badura-Skoda).
Other tension sources: thematic development, registral highs and lows, texture, and dissonance — ninth chords were heard as shocking (WTC II E major, bar 33; Chromatic Fugue bars 94, 135, 139, 158).
Some fugues have a different "fundamental line": a return to the beginning (BWV 548; WTC I C♯ major) or continual intensification (WTC I D♯ minor; most fugues with several subjects) — after Dürr.
sources: Badura-Skoda (1993), Ch. 9 pp. 204–209

topics.title: Proportion and spacing of entries
topics.summary: Count the length of each integrant and digression (in bars or beats) and look for patterns.
guidelines: Successive growth (BWV 578), mirror symmetry (BWV 533), or simple ratios 1:1, 2:1, 3:2, 4:3, 5:4 between sections (BWV 533, 545, 547).
Use "intuitive" ratios only (easy to picture), not 43:19.
sources: Roberts (2004), Ch. 3 Step 3; Ch. 4–7

topics.title: Gedalge's plan for an academic (school) fugue
topics.summary: The French conservatoire model: a fixed succession of sections with typical lengths. Useful as a yardstick — Bach's fugues rarely follow it.
guidelines: Compare a Bach fugue with this plan to see what is not "academic": Bach's strettos, key choices and endings are tailored to the subject (see the case studies).

tables.title: Plan for an academic fugue (lengths in bars)
rows: Subject or answer on the 2nd degree

sources: Gedalge, Traité de la fugue (plan table)

checks: Transcribed from the supplied one-page table

topics.title: The organ point (pedal) in fugues
topics.summary: A held or repeated bass under changing harmonies. Every source places it at the same structural moments.
rules: C. P. E. Bach: the organ point appears "generally in learned things, especially fugues, near the end over the dominant or over the final note"; occasionally mid-piece over the dominant or tonic of a key reached by modulation.
guidelines: Over a final dominant pedal composers bring "all manner of contrapuntal devices in stretto" (C. P. E. Bach) — the same place Marpurg prescribes for the closing stretti, and Gedalge for the dominant pedal before the final stretto.
Martini's four-part model ends with a stretto of subject and inverted countersubject over a three-bar bass pedal (Mann p. 280).
Historical root: Mersenne's point d'orgue was the fermata on the last note of a canonic voice (Mann p. 36).
In analysis, mark where pedals begin and end; a pedal often marks the arrival of the last section.
sources: C. P. E. Bach, Essay (trans. Mitchell 1949), ch. "The Organ Point"
Gedalge, Traité de la fugue (plan table)

checks: C. P. E. Bach, Marpurg (via Mann), Martini and Gedalge agree on dominant pedal before the close and tonic pedal at the end

topics.title: Hearing and showing the whole
topics.summary: Badura-Skoda's advice on turning an analysis into a performance.
guidelines: (C. P. E. Bach) When accompanying a fugue whose subject is in the bass, play the bass as written without chords until figures appear; a simple octave doubling of the bass suits loud fugal entries, but lively figuration is doubled only in its principal notes.
Aim for a "telescopic view" of the whole (filo, the connecting thread) while still shaping small units.
Think in lines, not chords: every voice is a melody, as if given to a string player; mark slurs and breaths per voice.
Do not "chisel out" every entry — exaggerating structure is like stressing the metre of a poem. Exceptions: strettos and close imitation, where the collision of voices is the message.
Complementary rhythm: accents in different voices fall at different times; cadential formulas are where accents coincide — the fugue's corner-stones.
Keep strict time inside sections; broaden only at structural breaks (pauses, imperfect cadences).
Thematic development (collocatio) asks for more tension than the exposition (in rhetorical terms).
sources: Badura-Skoda (1993), Ch. 9; Ch. 10 pp. 220–223
C. P. E. Bach, Essay (trans. Mitchell 1949), Part II: accompaniment §42; Ch. on the organ point

topics.title: Reading a subject's affect
topics.summary: Bach's fugues are expressive, not "abstract": subject, countersubjects and episodes all carry affect.
guidelines: Find the affect first; if unsure, compare with vocal works of similar material (arias, chorales) (Badura-Skoda).
Interval figures: 5̂–♭6̂–5̂ (minor 6th over the 5th) = pain/despair ("pathopoietic"); descending chromatic line = lament; diminished seventh = terror/tragedy (Badura-Skoda).
Bach's own slurs are rare; where they occur in subjects they usually mark sighs (pairs of descending seconds), e.g. the six slurs in the subject of WTC I B minor (Bodky).
Briskness → detached notes, tenderness → slurred broad notes, "in general" (C. P. E. Bach, quoted by Bodky).
sources: Badura-Skoda (1993), Ch. 9–10
Bodky (1960), Ch. 7 Articulation

checks: Slur counts in WTC subjects from Bodky's survey of autograph slurs

topics.title: Key character and symbols (with caution)
topics.summary: Some analysts read keys and figures symbolically. Treat these as hypotheses, not facts.
guidelines: Bodky compares pieces in the same key: e.g. E♭ major linked to the Trinity (three flats) and to the "fundamental" interval of the 4th; F minor to anguish; a C major tendency toward rising scales (after Abert).
Cross symbol: the subject of WTC I C♯ minor draws a cross and hides B-A-C-H (lines joining the middle notes and the outer notes form a cross — Hamel, quoted by Bodky).
Number symbolism: Badura-Skoda calls it a possible "self-imposed discipline", irrelevant to performance; the 13-note D♯ minor subject is an example of what such readings count.
sources: Bodky (1960), Ch. 8 Symbolism (Tonality Problems; Cross Symbols)
Badura-Skoda (1993), Ch. 9 p. 211

flags: Both authors warn against over-reading: Bodky notes Mattheson later withdrew his key descriptions and that Bach's keys in the WTC follow the scheme of all 24 keys; Badura-Skoda doubts cabbalistic readings of most works.

tools.title: Fugue analysis worksheet
tools.spec: A form the student fills in for any fugue: element map (entries with bar, voice, key, device), CS and episodes, then notable properties (checklist of Roberts' six types), integrant/digression lengths, and a verdict (rhetorical/literal) with reasons. Export as JSON/Markdown. Pre-filled demo: WTC I C minor from the case study.

tools.title: Proportion calculator
tools.spec: Enter section lengths (bars or beats); show them as a bar chart, flag successive growth/shrinking, palindromes, and ratios close to 1:1, 2:1, 3:2, 4:3, 5:4 (±10%). Demo data: BWV 578 digressions 2, 3, 3.5, 5, 8.5; BWV 533 spacing 2, 3.5, 3.5, 5, 5, 3.5, 3.5, 2.
